events.description: An authorized S3 team member executed a command intended to remove a small number of servers for an S3 subsystem used by the billing process; an input was entered incorrectly and a larger set of servers was removed than intended.

events.time: February 28, 2017, shortly after 9:37AM PST (implied by removal of capacity)
events.description: Removal of a significant portion of capacity caused the index and placement subsystems to require a full restart, and S3 became unable to service requests.

events.time: February 28, 2017, during the S3 disruption (no exact time given)
events.description: Other AWS services in US-EAST-1 relying on S3 were impacted, including the S3 console, EC2 new instance launches, EBS volumes needing S3 snapshot data, and AWS Lambda.

events.time: February 28, 2017, during subsystem restarts (no exact time given)
events.description: The restart process and safety checks to validate metadata integrity took longer than expected; the index subsystem was the first of the two to be restarted.

events.time: February 28, 2017, from the beginning of the event until 11:37AM PST
events.description: The team could not update service status on the AWS Service Health Dashboard due to its dependency on S3, so the AWS Twitter feed (@AWSCloud) and SHD banner text were used for communication.
The team regained the ability to update individual services' status on the Service Health Dashboard.
The index subsystem activated enough capacity to begin servicing S3 GET, LIST, and DELETE requests.
The index subsystem was fully recovered and GET, LIST, and DELETE APIs were functioning normally.

events.time: February 28, 2017, 1:18PM PST onward (when index subsystem was functional)
events.description: The placement subsystem began recovery, as it requires the index subsystem to be functioning properly.
The placement subsystem finished recovery and S3 was operating normally.

events.time: February 28, 2017, after S3 recovery (no exact time given)
events.description: Other impacted AWS services began recovering, with some requiring additional time to work through accumulated backlogs.
